text: Welcome to the Snowflake Data Engineering Capstone. Every course in this path taught you one piece on its own — Snowflake, dbt, Airflow, Power BI. This capstone ties all of them into one continuous platform, built for one company, end to end.

The company is Driftwood Media, a mid-size subscription streaming service. Leadership can't currently answer how many subscribers they gained last month, or what monthly recurring revenue is right now, without someone manually pulling numbers from three places: the billing platform's subscription events, the product app's usage logs, and a spreadsheet updated by hand before every leadership meeting.

Leadership asked for one thing, stated plainly: a single source of truth for subscriber growth, churn, and revenue, refreshed daily, that doesn't depend on anyone touching a spreadsheet. No real-time requirement, no machine learning — just a trustworthy, automated daily number.

The stack mirrors what a real Snowflake Developer or Analytics Engineer job posting actually asks for: Snowflake as the warehouse, dbt as the transformation layer, Airflow as the orchestrator, and Power BI as the reporting layer leadership actually opens every morning.

By the end, Driftwood will have raw data landing on schedule, a tested dbt project, an Airflow DAG running the daily sequence, a Power BI dashboard, subscriber PII protected with RBAC and masking, CI/CD testing every change, infrastructure provisioned with Terraform, an honest disaster-recovery posture, and a five-beat story you can tell an interviewer. Nothing here introduces a brand-new tool — every lesson applies something you've already used.
Next lesson: architecture planning — the full pipeline shape, the two-warehouse split, and the naming convention every later lesson follows.
